THE FIRST EXPECTATION WRITTEN HERE WAS DOWN, AND IT WAS WRONG — the model is right and the mechanism is worth stating. The realised price is a pass-through: it lifts revenue and direct cost by the same amount and leaves gross profit, which is volume x margin per litre, untouched. So it reaches value ONLY through working capital, which is struck off days ratios: the change is (receivable days + inventory days - payable days) / 365 x the change in revenue. Those days are about 34.5 + 19.8 - 85.2, which is NEGATIVE 31 days. A higher price therefore makes an already negative working-capital balance more negative, which RELEASES cash, and the value rises very slightly. The first expectation had the sign of the payable term backwards. Note how small the move is: this is a pass-through, and the model says so.

THE FIRST EXPECTATION WRITTEN HERE WAS DOWN, AND IT WAS WRONG. Work the waterfall through algebraically: free cash flow = NOPAT + depreciation - capital spending - the working-capital change, and NOPAT = (EBITDA - depreciation) x (1 - tax). Substituting gives free cash flow = EBITDA x (1 - tax) + depreciation x tax - capital spending - working capital. Depreciation does not cancel: it leaves a TAX SHIELD worth depreciation x the tax rate, so more depreciation RAISES free cash flow in the explicit years. It does lower terminal NOPAT, and therefore the terminal value, exactly as the first expectation said — but on these numbers the shield in the five explicit years slightly outweighs it. The net is small and positive, and the model is right.

THE SIGN LOOKS WRONG AND IS NOT. The spread is SUBTRACTED from the quoted yield to normalise it, so a larger spread means a LOWER normalised risk-free rate and a lower discount rate. That is the entire point of normalising: country risk is priced once, inside the equity premium, and stripping it from the yield is what stops it being counted twice.
